newsitem.title: hong kong: Britain, China agree pacts, ceremony, but still apart.
newsitem.headline: Britain, China agree pacts, ceremony, but still apart.

text.p: Britain and China agreed on Friday to keep intact over 200 treaties between Hong Kong and the world, and put finishing touches on a joint ceremony to mark Hong Kong's return to Beijing's control on July 1.
But, after three days of diplomatic talks in a final bargaining round before the big event, there was little sign of harmony on other problems connected to the historic handover.
Hong Kong after 156 years of British colonial rule reverts to China as a Special Administrative Region (SAR) with considerable autonomy, retaining its status as a capitalist bastion.
The Hong Kong government unveiled impressive economic figures to demonstrate that consumer confidence remains high.
Statistics for the first three months of the year portrayed the economy steaming steadily ahead while inflation showed signs of easing.
And on the stock exchange Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index of blue chip shares gained 341-points to a fresh record close of 14,757.81.
Underlining a prospective change without any exact parallel in history, more advance troops of the People's Liberation Army entered this territory of 6.4 million people at the southern tip of China.
The arrival of 90 servicemen almost doubled Beijing's advance guard in Hong Kong to gear up for the merger with China in 32 days time. The garrison is eventually expected to be up to 10,000 strong.
Future Hong Kong leader Tung Chee-hwa urged activists not to upset China by making the territory a base for subverting the communist-ruled country.

He told pro-democracy campaigners to forget mourning China's bloody 1989 Tiananmen crackdown, when army tanks crushed student-led pro-democracy protests with a heavy loss of life. The June 4 anniversary regularly draws tens of thousands of protesters on the streets of Hong Kong.
More diplomatic wrangling with some progress this time marked the latest session of the Sino-British Joint Liaison Group (JLG).

"We reached a consensus on the application of more than 200 international treaties... The two sides also resolved the participation of the SAR in international organisations," Zhao Jihua, senior Chinese representative told a news conference.

British senior representative Hugh Davies confirmed the statement in a separate news conference, adding that the two sides made some headway on 21 air service agreements between Hong Kong and other countries.
They also said they agreed on details of the handover ceremony and a guest list of 3,600, mostly of foreign minister rank and 400 journalists.

Davies said all 15 member countries of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum (APEC), 14 members of the European Union and 16 others with links to Hong Kong, such as India, Egypt, Russia and Saudi Arabia, had been invited.
However, Zhao declined to say whether Chinese President Jiang Zemin would attend the ceremony, where Britain's chief representative will be royal heir Prince Charles.
Zhao also urged Britain to adopt an attitude of "positive cooperation" in resolving a transfer of archives and government assets in the remaining month.

As for London's future role on Hong Kong, Zhao said the territory's affairs were internal matters of China and that Britain had no right to interfere through the JLG, which will continue to operate until the year 2000.
